options.text: Equilibrium quantity must fall.
Equilibrium price must rise.
Equilibrium price must fall.
Both price and quantity are unchanged.
options.misconception: selects "Both price and quantity are unchanged" instead of "Equilibrium quantity must fall"

questions.explanation: For a curve shifts question like this, the governing rule is: Quantity falls under both shifts. Applying it makes "Equilibrium quantity must fall" correct. The alternative "Equilibrium price must rise" is wrong because it price is indeterminate.
questions.hint: Quantity falls under both shifts.

questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.stem: A per-unit tax is imposed on buyers of transit rides. What happens to demand?

options.text: Demand shifts right as buyers seek more.
options.misconception: confuses "Demand shifts right as buyers seek more" with the correct "Demand shifts left as the effective price to buyers rises"

options.text: Demand shifts left as the effective price to buyers rises.
Supply shifts left as sellers pay more.
Nothing changes until sellers react.
options.misconception: confuses "Nothing changes until sellers react" with the correct "Demand shifts left as the effective price to buyers rises"

questions.explanation: The rule that settles this tax incidence item is: Buyers face a higher effective price. That is why "Demand shifts left as the effective price to buyers rises" is right. The option "Demand shifts right as buyers seek more" (confuses "Demand shifts right as buyers seek more" with the correct "Demand shifts left as the effective price to buyers rises") does not satisfy the rule.
questions.hint: Buyers face a higher effective price.

questions.stem: A minimum fare is set below the equilibrium fare.

options.text: The floor binds and creates surplus.

options.text: Quantity supplied falls to the floor.
The floor is non-binding and nothing changes.
A shortage results at the floor.

questions.explanation: Applying the price floors rule — Compare floor to equilibrium price — yields "The floor is non-binding and nothing changes". The tempting "The floor binds and creates surplus" fails because it names "The floor binds and creates surplus" where the rule requires "The floor is non-binding and nothing changes".
questions.hint: Compare floor to equilibrium price.

questions.learningObjective: Predict demand shift from income fall
questions.stem: A consulting note on demand changes presents the evidence set out below. Rider incomes fall during a recession.

options.text: Demand shifts left as riders cut spending.
This is a movement along demand.
Supply shifts left as agencies lose revenue.
Demand shifts right as riders seek cheaper transit.
options.misconception: confuses "Demand shifts right as riders seek cheaper transit" with the correct "Demand shifts left as riders cut spending"

questions.explanation: For a demand changes question like this, the governing rule is: Income fell, so demand shifts. Applying it makes "Demand shifts left as riders cut spending" correct. The alternative "Demand shifts right as riders seek cheaper transit" is wrong because it confuses "Demand shifts right as riders seek cheaper transit" with the correct "Demand shifts left as riders cut spending".
questions.hint: Income fell, so demand shifts.

questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.stem: Explain how a surplus is eliminated in a competitive market.

answer.exemplar: Sellers with excess stock cut price; lower price raises quantity demanded and reduces quantity supplied until equilibrium.

questions.explanation: The rule that settles this equilibrium adjustment item is: Surplus leads sellers to cut price. That is why "Sellers with excess stock cut price; lower price raises quantity demanded and reduces quantity supplied until equilibrium" is the answer.
questions.hint: Surplus leads sellers to cut price.

questions.stem: Cross-price elasticity between bus and train fares is +1.2. Are they substitutes or complements?
questions.explanation: Applying the substitutes and complements rule — Positive cross-price means substitutes — yields "1". Reversing the reasoning would recover the given quantities.
questions.hint: Positive cross-price means substitutes.

questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.stem: Explain the difference between a movement along and a shift of the demand curve.

answer.exemplar: A movement along demand is caused by a price change; a shift is caused by a non-price determinant like income or tastes.

questions.explanation: The laws of demand and supply principle here is: Price change versus non-price change. On that basis "A movement along demand is caused by a price change; a shift is caused by a non-price determinant like income or tastes" is correct.
questions.hint: Price change versus non-price change.

questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.stem: Equilibrium price is 10. A $3 tax on sellers shifts supply up by 3. New equilibrium price to buyers is?
questions.explanation: The rule that settles this equilibrium item is: Add the tax to the original price. That is why "12" is the answer.
questions.hint: Add the tax to the original price.

questions.stem: A transit campaign advertises the convenience of buses.

options.text: Supply shifts right as more buses run.
Demand shifts right as tastes favor buses.
Demand shifts left as riders feel pressured.
options.misconception: names "Demand shifts left as riders feel pressured" where the rule requires "Demand shifts right as tastes favor buses"

options.text: This is a movement along demand.

questions.explanation: Applying the demand shifters rule — Advertising changes tastes — yields "Demand shifts right as tastes favor buses". The tempting "Supply shifts right as more buses run" fails because it confuses advertising with production.
questions.hint: Advertising changes tastes.

questions.stem: Bus operators expect higher fares next month and reduce service now.

options.text: Demand shifts left as riders anticipate.
Supply shifts right as operators expand.
options.misconception: names "Supply shifts right as operators expand" where the rule requires "Supply shifts left as sellers withhold output"

options.text: Supply shifts left as sellers withhold output.
This is a movement along supply.

questions.explanation: The supply shifters principle here is: Sellers expect higher prices later. On that basis "Supply shifts left as sellers withhold output" is correct, while "Demand shifts left as riders anticipate" confuses expectations with demand.
questions.hint: Sellers expect higher prices later.

questions.stem: At a fare of $5, quantity demanded is 800 and quantity supplied is 650. What is the shortage?
questions.explanation: For a disequilibrium question like this, the governing rule is: Subtract supplied from demanded. Applying it gives "150" as the answer.

questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.stem: Supply shifts left while demand stays fixed. What happens to price?

options.text: Price falls and quantity rises.
options.misconception: selects "Price falls and quantity rises" instead of "Price rises and quantity falls"

options.text: Price and quantity are unchanged.
options.misconception: confuses "Price and quantity are unchanged" with the correct "Price rises and quantity falls"

options.text: Price rises and quantity rises.
Price rises and quantity falls.

questions.explanation: A leftward supply shift with demand fixed raises price and lowers the quantity traded. Reversing the effect, leaving both unchanged, or copying the prediction for a demand shift all miss that supply is what moved.
questions.hint: Less supply means higher price.

questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.stem: Demand is more elastic than supply. Who bears more of a tax?

options.text: Sellers bear more because supply is less elastic.
Buyers bear more because demand is elastic.
options.misconception: names "Buyers bear more because demand is elastic" where the rule requires "Sellers bear more because supply is less elastic"

options.text: Both bear equal shares.
options.misconception: selects "Both bear equal shares" instead of "Sellers bear more because supply is less elastic"

options.text: The government bears it all.

questions.explanation: Applying the tax incidence rule — Less elastic means more burden — yields "Sellers bear more because supply is less elastic". The tempting "Buyers bear more because demand is elastic" fails because it names "Buyers bear more because demand is elastic" where the rule requires "Sellers bear more because supply is less elastic".
questions.hint: Less elastic means more burden.

questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.stem: Explain why a binding price floor can waste resources.

answer.exemplar: A binding floor creates surplus units that are produced but not bought, wasting labor and materials on unneeded output.

questions.explanation: The price floors principle here is: Surplus units still cost resources. On that basis "A binding floor creates surplus units that are produced but not bought, wasting labor and materials on unneeded output" is correct.
questions.hint: Surplus units still cost resources.

questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.stem: Explain why a binding price ceiling causes non-price rationing.

answer.exemplar: With price fixed below equilibrium, quantity demanded exceeds supply, so sellers ration by queues, favoritism, or black markets.

questions.explanation: For a price ceilings question like this, the governing rule is: Price cannot clear the market. Applying it gives "With price fixed below equilibrium, quantity demanded exceeds supply, so sellers ration by queues, favoritism, or black markets" as the answer.
questions.hint: Price cannot clear the market.

questions.stem: Transit rides are a normal good. What happens to demand when incomes rise?

questions.hint: Normal good means demand rises with income.

questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.stem: Explain why a price rise in one good can raise demand for another.

answer.exemplar: If two goods are substitutes, a higher price in one pushes consumers toward the other, raising its demand.

questions.explanation: For a substitutes and complements question like this, the governing rule is: Substitutes replace each other. Applying it gives "If two goods are substitutes, a higher price in one pushes consumers toward the other, raising its demand" as the answer.
questions.hint: Substitutes replace each other.
